newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian actor Mastroianni dies in Paris.
newsitem.headline: Italian actor Mastroianni dies in Paris.

text.p: Actor Marcello Mastroianni, Italy's quintessential Latin Lover and the symbol of the Dolce Vita, died at his home in Paris on Thursday, aged 72.
His Italian agent Giovanna Cau said Mastroianni passed away on Thursday morning and gave no cause of death. Italian media said he had been suffering from cancer of the pancreas.
In some 160 films, starring alongside many of cinema's most beautiful women, Mastroianni became an enduring symbol of suave Latin sex appeal.

He had his first international success in 1960 in director Federico Fellini's "La Dolce Vita", whose scene of a young Mastroianni splashing in the Trevi Fountain in Rome with Swedish blonde Anita Ekberg is one of cinema's indelible images.
The city of Rome said it would turn off the water at the fountain, douse the lights and drape the monument in black cloth at five p.m. (1600 GMT) as a mark of respect.
The actor went on to star in many of Fellini's other works, as recently as the late director's 1986 film "Ginger and Fred", while never losing a reputation for modesty.
"When I was a kid...I had a chest that looked like a basket and two bird's legs," Mastroianni once said.
"I'm not handsome and I never have been."

French radio stations said Mastroianni's companion, French actress Catherine Deneuve, their daughter Chiara and actor Michel Piccoli were at his side when he died. His daughter Barbara from an earlier marriage also was present, Cau said.

"Marcello was the sweetest, nicest, most light-hearted actor, a great friend who I will miss a lot," said actress Monica Vitti, who starred with Mastroianni in Michelangelo Antonioni's 1961 film "The Night" and other films.
Italian director Mario Monicelli, who cast Mastroianni in his renowned film "I Soliti Ignoti" in 1958, described the actor as "devoid of celebrity affectations...and graciously ironic".
Italian radio, reporting from Paris, said Mastroianni had died at dawn and that friends, including many from the film world, went to his house in the French capital to pay respects.
The Italian news agency ANSA said his funeral would be held in Rome with a small private ceremony in Paris. It gave no dates for either event.

Apart from "La Dolce Vita", Mastroianni perhaps will be best remembered for films in which he starred with Sophia Loren such as "Marriage Italian Style", "The Priest's Wife", "Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow", "Sunflowers" and "A Special Day."
Mastroianni, who shunned publicity and rarely granted interviews, was born to peasant parents on September 28, 1924, at Fontana Liri, a mountain hamlet southeast of Rome.
When he was still a boy the family moved to the northern industrial city of Turin and then to Rome, where Marcello earned a degree in surveying and planned to become an architect.

At 19, he was picked up by Nazi troops who had occupied Rome and sent to a forced labour camp in northern Italy. He escaped to Venice, where he drew pictures of the lagoon city's landmarks and sold them to tourists for food.

After the war he returned to Rome, where he worked as a clerk in the accounting department of the British Eagle-Lion film company and in the evenings began acting with a Rome University theatrical company.
In 1947 he made his screen debut in the Italian version of "Les Miserables" and a year later made his stage debut in a play which starred Giulietta Masina, Fellini's wife.
It was an acquaintanceship that changed his life but, said his friends, not his ways.
"He was a man who never once made a television advert," said Italian journalist Enzo Biagi, a friend who said Mastroianni had told him recently that he had cancer.
"That was the way he was," Biagi said. "Nice, normal, not a diva at all."
